info.bio: Aunque muchos la recordarán por haber escrito junto a Jack Niztsche “Up Where We Belong”, canción que le valió un Óscar y que Joe Cocker y Jennifer Warnes convirtieron en banda sonora de “Oficial y caballero”, la canadiense Buffy Sainte-Marie es cualquier cosa menos una “one hit wonder”. Cantante, compositora, activista social y artista visual, entre muchas otras cosas, Sainte-Marie es también una figura clave de la música americana de las últimas décadas

scenes.name: Berkeley y la protesta contra la guerra
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En septiembre de 1964 las autoridades de la Universidad de California intentaron prohibir los mítines por los derechos civiles; la sentada que siguió, con la retórica de Mario Savio («poned vuestros cuerpos sobre los engranajes»), se convirtió en el Free Speech Movement. En mayo de 1965 Jerry Rubin y Abbie Hoffman, entre otros, fundaron el Vietnam Day Committee, que piqueteó los trenes de tropas de Oakland bajo el lema «Make Love Not War». Hubo marcha del SDS y el SNCC en Washington, quema de cartillas de reclutamiento (castigada desde agosto de 1965 con cinco años de cárcel) y grandes manifestaciones el 15 de octubre. De ese fermento salió «I Feel Like I’m Fixin’ to Die Rag» de Country Joe McDonald (Rag Baby, octubre de 1965), un ragtime para marchar que culpa a generales, a Wall Street y a los padres crédulos, no a los soldados. Phil Ochs ironizó con «Draft Dodger Rag». En enero de 1966 Ronald Reagan hizo de los disturbios de Berkeley, «un carnaval de pesadilla», el eje de su campaña a gobernador.

podcast.title: Academy Award-Winning Songwriter
podcast.body: In 1982, Buffy Sainte-Marie won an Academy Award, a Golden Globe, and a BAFTA for the song "Up Where We Belong," which was performed by Joe Cocker and Jennifer Warnes for the film *An Officer and a Gentleman*. "In 1982, she won an Academy Award and a Golden Globe and a BAFTA for the song Up Were We Belong, which was sung by Joe Cocker and Jennifer Warren's in the movie An Officer in A Gentlemen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Adoption and Mi'kmaq Upbringing
podcast.body: Although a member of the Piapot Plains Cree First Nation, Buffy was adopted and grew up in Massachusetts, with her adoptive parents being of Mi'kmaq descent, connecting her to multiple Indigenous traditions. "She is a member of the Piappot Plains Cree First Nation, but then she was adopted and grew up in Massachusetts, and those adopted parents were of Mick Mack to set."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Birth and Early Activism
podcast.body: Buffy Sainte-Marie was born in the Qu'Appelle Valley in Saskatchewan in 1941 and has been an activist for native causes for as long as she can remember, using her platform to advocate for Indigenous rights. "Buffy was born in the Capell Valley in Saskatchewan in 1941, and she's been an activist for native causes for as long as she can remember."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Blacklisted by Nixon Administration
podcast.body: Buffy St. Marie was blacklisted by the Nixon administration for 15 years due to writing "songs about truth," leading to her absence from the music business. "She was blacklisted by the Nixon administration for writing songs about truth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Covered by Renowned Artists
podcast.body: Her songs were covered by numerous other artists, including Janis Joplin, Donovan, and much later, Courtney Love, demonstrating the widespread appeal and influence of her songwriting. "Other people started covering her songs. Janice Joplin, Donovan and even much later of course, Courtney Love."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Online Collaboration Pioneer
podcast.body: For her album "Coincidence and Likely Stories," Buffy St. Marie, living in Hawaii, collaborated with Chris Berkett in London by sending MIDI files of her keyboard parts via Compuserve (a dial-in modem service before the World Wide Web). This pioneering method allowed the album to be "born on the web." "So Roger managed to get her MIDI files onto the Compuserve and I managed to work out and download them via Compuserve into my system in London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Awards and Honors
podcast.body: Buffy Sainte-Marie has received numerous honorary doctorates, Juno Awards, and Hall of Fame Awards, underscoring her vast contributions to music and culture. "And I can go on with all the honorary doctorates, the June Awards, the Hall of Fame Awards, all the other sort of awards."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nihewan Foundation Founder
podcast.body: She founded the non-profit organization, the Nihewan Foundation for the American Indian, which focuses on reaching out to young people from tribes across North America and as far as Hawaii. "She has a non-profit called the Nehewan Foundation for the American Indian, which reaches out to young people from tribes all across North America and even out to Hawaii."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Polaris Music Prize Winner
podcast.body: In 2015, at the age of 74, Buffy Sainte-Marie won the Polaris Music Prize for her album "Power in the Blood," a testament to her enduring artistic relevance and impact. "In 2015, at the age of 74, she won the Polaris Music Prize for her album Power in the Blood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Red Power Movement Voice
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, Buffy Sainte-Marie became the leading female voice in the Red Power Movement, an effort to make the plight of Native Americans heard, which she noted led to her being banned from some radio stations. "In the early 70s, she was the leading female voice in the effort to make a plight of Native Americans heard. This was known as the Red Power Movement, something she said got her banned from some radio stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sesame Street Regular
podcast.body: She was a regular on the children's television show *Sesame Street*, where she taught kids about native culture, bringing Indigenous traditions and perspectives to a young, mainstream audience. "She became a regular on Sesame Street, teaching kids about native culture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sesame Street Work
podcast.body: During her 15-year hiatus from the music business, Buffy St. Marie worked on "Sesame Street." "She'd been out of the business. She'd been doing Sesame Street for 15 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Visual Artist
podcast.body: Beyond her music, Buffy Sainte-Marie is also a visual artist, with her work featured in exhibitions and galleries across North America. "She's also a visual artist who is at exhibitions and galleries all across North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocal Recording at Walter Becker's Studio
podcast.body: Since Buffy St. Marie did not have a 24-track machine in her home studio, Chris Berkett had to transport 15 heavy 24-track tapes in a flight case to Walter Becker's studio in Maui to record her vocals and other parts. "I had to take a flight case full of like 1524 tracks. Really heavy. Over to Walter Becker studio, Stevie Dan studio in Maui because Buffy didn't have a 24 track machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Yorkville Folk Scene Pioneer
podcast.body: In the 1960s, she developed her skills as a singer-songwriter and was a regular presence in Toronto's Yorkville District folk scene, alongside other emerging talents like Neil Young, Leonard Cohen, Joni Mitchell, and John Kay. "In the 1960s, she developed as a singer-songwriter in Hangout and Toronto's Yorkville District at the same time as Neil Young and Leonard Cohen and Joni Mitchell and John Kaye, who would later form Steppenwolf and many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Buffy Sainte-Marie
xref.body: She provided vocals on the song "You Got to Run" from Buffy Sainte-Marie's 2017 album "Medicine Songs," bringing together two Polaris Prize-winning Indigenous Canadian artists. "This double shot is called You Got to Run. Two Indigenous Canadians, two Polaris Prize winners, Buffy St. Marie and Tanya Tagak, together on a 2017 song called You Got to Run."
